news.title: Windows Update Triggers a Crash — The October Patch is Here
news.excerpt: Microsoft confirmed this week that a October 2026 Windows update can cause some programs and games to crash when they play certain sound files. The problem only hits a narrow set of audio paths — not every machine — but if you installed updates in the last 48 hours and noticed sudden crashes, that's likely it. Don't reinstall anything, don't roll back your drivers, and don't call support yet. Microsoft is shipping a fix in the next update, expected within days. The honest answer is that these bugs are real, they're temporary, and the correct move is to wait for the patch rather than chase the problem with a new install.

news.title: A Big Online Store Got Hacked — Change That Password
news.excerpt: A hacker broke into ASOS, the big online clothing store, and walked off with customer information. The company confirmed the break-in this week after shoppers started seeing strange messages. If you have an ASOS account, change that password today — and never reuse it anywhere else. Crooks who steal one password try it on your email and your bank next. I've had customers lose an account for exactly this reason. Two minutes now saves a world of grief.

news.title: That 'I'm Not a Robot' Box Is a Trick
news.excerpt: Fake "I'm not a robot" boxes are showing up in search results and on random websites. They look harmless, but they tell you to press a few keys and paste something into a little box to prove you're a person. Do that and you've just started a bad program on your computer. Real checks never ask you to press keys or paste anything — so close the tab. I've had two machines come in this month with exactly this. According to a new report, most now arrive straight from search results.

news.title: A Code You Didn't Ask For — Don't Type It In
news.excerpt: There's a new way crooks get into your computer and your online accounts without ever learning your password. You get a message with a short code and a link to a real-looking Microsoft or Google page, telling you to type the code in to "confirm" or "protect" your account. Do that, and you've just let them in. My rule is simple: never type a code you didn't ask for. Got one? Delete the message — that's the whole fix.

news.title: Fake FBI Agents Are Calling — Hang Up and Check
news.excerpt: Crooks are making fake calls, saying they are FBI, DEA, or Secret Service agents. They make a real agency's phone number show up on your screen and use a real agent's name, then push you to move your money to keep it "safe." The FBI says never send money to anyone claiming to be a federal agent. If this happens to you, it's a scam — hang up and call the agency yourself at a number you look up. I've had two customers ask me about calls like this just this week.

posts.title: Apple just shipped a new iPhone security update that closes a flaw people were already attacked with — install it free at Settings > General > Software Update
posts.summary: Pick up your iPhone, open Settings → General → Software Update, and tap Update Now. Apple's newest security update fixes a hole that has already been used in real attacks against real people, not just a theoretical problem. It takes about 10 minutes on Wi-Fi and it's completely free. Do it tonight.
posts.truth: Most people tap "Remind Me Later" on updates until the phone is a year behind. The honest answer is that security updates are the cheapest insurance you will ever get, and the ones Apple sends out of the blue — like this one — are the ones that actually matter. I see this all the time: a phone holding a banking app, an email inbox, and every family photo, still running software with a known hole that bad guys have already walked through. They don't need a clever trick when the door was left open.

posts.title: Need to split or combine a PDF? Firefox's free built-in PDF editor does it at firefox.com — no Adobe needed
posts.summary: Update Firefox free at firefox.com (or click Menu → Help → About to get the newest version). Open any PDF in Firefox, click the little page-thumbnail icon in the top-left corner, and you get a toolbar that can split, merge, reorder, rotate, and add pages. Then save it. You never upload the file to a website and you never pay a subscription — it all happens on your own computer.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize the PDF they're afraid to open is something they could already handle. I see this all the time — someone paying about $20 a month for Adobe just to rotate one scanned page or combine two forms. The honest answer is that you've already paid for a browser once, and Firefox can now edit PDFs for free. Because it happens right on your machine, your tax return, your medical form, or your bank statement never has to be handed to some stranger's website.

posts.title: Microsoft is turning on a free Windows safety feature called Core isolation this month — check yours at Windows Security > Device security
posts.summary: Click Start, type Windows Security, and open it. Choose Device security, then click Core isolation details and look at the switch under Core isolation. Microsoft started switching this protection on automatically this month, through the ordinary Windows updates your computer already gets — but not every computer qualifies. If yours is off, turn it on and restart. It is built into Windows, it is free, and there is nothing to buy.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize the nastiest attacks aren't the ones you can see — they are programs that quietly tamper with the deepest part of Windows so nothing can get a clean look at them. October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and the honest answer is that the best protection you have was already sitting inside your computer, switched off. It is one switch and one restart, and nobody has to pay for it.

posts.title: Read any web page without the clutter — Microsoft Edge's free Reading mode strips the ads and reads it aloud, just press F9
posts.summary: Open the article in Microsoft Edge and press F9, or click the little open-book icon at the right end of the address bar. Edge calls it Reading mode — it hides the ads, the pop-ups, and the "you might also like" clutter, leaving just the words in a bigger, cleaner type. If you'd rather listen, click Read aloud on the small toolbar that appears and the computer reads the whole page to you. It is built into Edge, it is free, and there is nothing to download.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize the reason a simple recipe or news story is so hard to read isn't their eyes — it's the website. The page is fighting for your attention with ads and videos, and it wins. The honest answer is that you don't have to fight back by zooming and squinting: the browser already has a calm, quiet version of every page, and it's one key away.

posts.title: Sound and look better on video calls — a Logitech webcam with a built-in microphone is about 40 dollars at logitech.com or Amazon
posts.summary: Buy a Logitech webcam — the C270 is about 40 dollars and the C920 is about 60 — from logitech.com, Amazon, or Walmart. Plug the USB cable into your computer and you're done; there's nothing to install on Windows or a Mac. You get a much sharper picture and a microphone that doesn't echo, so family, doctors, and work calls can actually see and hear you.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize the camera built into a laptop was the cheapest part the maker could buy. That's why you look dim, grainy, and washed out while the person you're talking to looks fine — they have a better camera, not a better face. The honest answer is that a 40-dollar webcam is one of the biggest quality-of-life upgrades a home computer can get, and it plugs into a USB port in five seconds.

I see this all the time: a customer apologizes for "looking bad" on every video call. It's never them. It's the camera.

posts.title: Speed up a sluggish Windows PC for free with Microsoft PC Manager — Microsoft's own one-click cleaner, at pcmanager.microsoft.com
posts.summary: Download Microsoft PC Manager free from pcmanager.microsoft.com or from the Microsoft Store (search "Microsoft PC Manager"). Open it and click Cleanup — it sweeps out junk files, shows you which programs are slowing your startup, and runs Microsoft's own virus scan, all from one window. No subscription, no account needed, and no pop-up ads after every click.
posts.truth: I do not use the paid "PC cleaners" that show up in ads — most of them are the very thing slowing the machine down. The honest answer is that the best free cleanup tool for Windows is made by the people who built Windows. I see this all the time: a computer with three different "speed booster" programs fighting each other while the real junk just sits there untouched. One clean tool from a name you trust beats five from names you've never heard of.

posts.title: Stop reusing one password everywhere — Proton Pass is the free password manager that fills in your logins, at proton.me/pass
posts.summary: Go to proton.me/pass and create a free account. Proton Pass remembers every password, makes up strong new ones for you, and fills them in automatically on your computer. The free plan has no limit on how many passwords you can store, and you only have to remember the one that unlocks the app.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that "I use the same password everywhere" is exactly how one leaked website turns into ten hacked accounts. If the same password protects your email, someone who steals it can reset everything else — and that is the account a scammer wants most. When a customer is ready, I install Proton Pass on their computer and we move the logins over a few at a time, starting with email and banking. The honest answer is that the fix takes one afternoon, and then you never think about it again.

posts.title: Computer prices are way up this year because of AI — before you buy anything new, run the free Crucial System Scanner at crucial.com
posts.summary: Open your browser and go to crucial.com. Click the System Scanner link, download the free tool, and run it. In about two minutes it reads your exact make and model, shows what parts you already have, and tells you the most your computer can hold. No account, no cost, nothing to sign up for. That way you know what you own before you walk into a store or hand over a credit card.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize why a new computer costs so much more this year. It isn't the shop and it isn't the government — the big AI data centers are buying up memory chips and storage by the truckload, and prices on parts and finished machines have climbed a lot. The honest answer is that this is the worst year in a long time to buy new, and most folks who think they need a new computer really don't.

posts.title: Type a few words and get a picture — Microsoft Designer's free AI Image Creator makes birthday cards and posters at designer.microsoft.com
posts.summary: In any browser go to designer.microsoft.com, sign in with a free Microsoft account (the same one you use for email, if you have it), and type what you want to see — "a birthday card for my granddaughter who loves horses," or "a flyer for our church fish fry on Saturday." Click Create and a few seconds later you'll have finished-looking pictures you can download, print, or share. It is free to use, and you don't need to know anything about art or computers.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize they can make a card or a flyer that looks store-bought without buying one single thing. They figure good design is for people with a talent or an expensive program. The honest answer is that you describe it in plain English and the computer draws it — then you print it on the printer you already own.

posts.title: Type and click without touching the keyboard — Windows Voice Access is built into Windows 11, free at Settings > Accessibility > Speech
posts.summary: Open Settings > Accessibility > Speech and turn on Voice access. Then just talk: say "open my email," "click Save," or "type Dear Mary" and Windows does it for you. It's built into Windows 11, costs nothing, needs no account, and works even without internet. If your hands ache, your keyboard is acting up, or you'd simply rather talk than type, this turns your computer into a hands-free machine.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize Windows already has a full voice-control feature — they picture expensive software or a subscription, so they never look. It's sitting right there in Settings. It won't read your mind, and you do have to speak a little clearly, but for anyone whose hands hurt or who types slowly, it's the difference between fighting the computer and just using it.

I see this all the time: someone with arthritis or a recovering wrist injury, quietly struggling every day. Two minutes in Settings changes their whole afternoon.
